# ReDeEP: Detecting Hallucination in Retrieval-Augmented Generation via Mechanistic Interpretability

## Summary

- **Background**: In RAG, a model can contradict a retrieved document that is correct and relevant, which the authors call RAG Hallucination. They separate this from Knowledge Conflict, because a conflict between the context and parametric knowledge does not always produce a hallucination.
- **Gap**: The authors sort existing detectors into three causal groups: PCE, ECP and MPE. They argue that none of the three separates the model's use of external context from its use of parametric knowledge.
- **Research Question**: Which internal components are linked to RAG hallucinations? Can a detector that scores those components separately beat existing detectors?
- **Methods**: A correlational and interventional study of attention heads and FFNs in Llama2-7B-chat on the RAGTruth training set. This produces ReDeEP, a weighted difference of FFN-based PKS and head-based ECS, tested on RAGTruth and Dolly (AC) with three LLaMA models against 16 baselines.
- **Key Findings**:
    - On Llama2-7B, 1006 of 1024 heads score higher ECS on truthful responses, and later-layer FFNs add more parametric knowledge on hallucinated responses.
    - ReDeEP has the best AUC in all six model × dataset cells, but on RAGTruth its lead over the best baseline is only about 0.015–0.04.
    - AARF wins more GPT-4o pairwise truthfulness judgements than the unmodified model, but the text gives no counts.
- **Limitations**:
    - The mechanism was found in one model, and the "causal" test only shows that disrupting these components raises NLL on truthful responses.
    - The ablation shows ECS alone does almost all of the work, so the decoupling argument rests on small increments.
    - The best variant, ReDeEP(chunk), scores context use with an external BGE embedding model, so its gains are not purely internal-mechanism signals.

## Details

### What the two scores measure

Both scores are proxies the authors designed themselves. They concede the metrics "may not be exact" (§3.1, p. 5).

- **External Context Score (ECS)**, per head and per token (§3.1, p. 4–5). Take the top 10% of context tokens by the head's attention weight. Mean-pool their last-layer hidden states. ECS is the cosine similarity between that pooled vector and the current token's last-layer hidden state. A response's ECS is the average over its tokens. The score blends two things the paper later wants to tell apart: whether the head attended to the right tokens, and whether that information survived into the final layer.
- **Parametric Knowledge Score (PKS)**, per layer (Eq. 5). This is the JSD between the LogitLens vocabulary distributions of the residual stream before and after the FFN. It measures how much the FFN changes the next-token distribution. Calling that change "parametric knowledge" is an interpretation borrowed from Geva et al., not something the paper measures.
- **Copying head score** (Appendix B). Elhage et al.'s count of positive eigenvalues is replaced by a heuristic: the trace of $W_U W_{OV} W_E$, Gershgorin disks, IQR outlier counts and a rank sum. The paper does not check this heuristic against the exact eigenvalue method. "Copying Heads" in this paper therefore means heads ranked by this approximation.

### The mechanistic evidence

All of §3 uses Llama2-7B-chat on the RAGTruth training set. The number of truthful and hallucinated responses is not given in the text.

- **RQ1, external context.** 1006 of 1024 heads have $\Delta E > 0$ (truthful minus hallucinated), and most heads' ECS correlates negatively with the hallucination label (Fig. 4a–b, p. 6). Per-head copying scores correlate with these maps at PCC 0.41 and 0.46 (Fig. 4c). This is the basis for saying that "heads associated with hallucinations are often Copying Heads". A correlation of around 0.4 across heads supports "tend to be", not "are".
- **RQ1, parametric knowledge.** Later-layer FFNs have higher PKS on hallucinated responses and correlate positively with the label (Fig. 4d–e). The authors then *define* these layers as "Knowledge FFNs". The category is picked out by its correlation with hallucination, so its link to hallucination is partly true by construction.
- **Lost versus mis-attended (Appendix C, Table 2).** On responses Llama2-7B got wrong, the context span with the highest mean attention was checked by GPT-4o: could it support the annotated conflict? It could in 77.5% of cases. The authors take this to mean that hallucinations come mainly from the model *losing* information the heads attended to. That is an inference: the check shows only that attention landed on the relevant span, and it rests on a single GPT-4o judgement per item. They propose copy-suppression heads (McDougall et al.) as a possible cause, but do not test it.
- **RQ2, "causal" intervention (Appendix D).** Two interventions: replace the attention scores of the top 32 Copying Heads with $\mathcal{N}(0,1)$ noise, and multiply the top 5 Knowledge FFNs' contributions by 10. Each is compared with matched control heads or layers. The outcome is the change in NLL on *truthful* responses, and the experimental groups shift NLL more (Fig. 5 left). The text gives no numbers. What this shows is that these components matter more for reproducing faithful text than nearby ones do. It does not show that their natural variation causes hallucination, and hallucination rate is never the outcome.
- **RQ3 (Appendix E).** Llama2-7B answered the truthful-set queries without retrieval, and GPT-4o kept the answers matching the reference as the "LLM-known" set $\hat{D}_T$. Compared with $D_H$, this set has higher ECS and lower PKS (Fig. 5 right). The two sets differ in query, task and response at the same time, so this is a contrast between groups, not a controlled comparison.
- **Authors' reading.** They link the FFN result to early-exit work (DoLa, CALM): when the context is sufficient, shallow layers suffice, and deeper parametric additions "confuse" the model (p. 7). This is offered as consistency with prior work and not tested here.

### From mechanism to detector

- **ReDeEP(token)** (§4.1): $H_t(t)=\sum_{l\in F}\alpha P^l_t-\sum_{(l,h)\in A}\beta E^{l,h}_t$, averaged over the response. The paper calls α and β "regression coefficients", and the text after the equation swaps which one belongs to which score. In the implementation, α = 1 throughout and β, the number of top heads and the number of top FFN layers are chosen on the RAGTruth validation set. On Dolly (AC) they are chosen by "twofold validation" (Appendix I). So the detector is a weighted difference tuned by hand, not a fitted regression model.
- **The selected configurations vary a lot.** Heads range from top-1 to top-11, FFN layers from top-1 to top-30, and β from 0.1 to 1.8 across models, datasets and variants (Appendix I). There is no stable "Copying Head / Knowledge FFN" set that carries over between settings.
- **ReDeEP(chunk)** (§4.2): the context and response are split with LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter. For each response chunk, the context chunk with the highest mean attention is found, and ECS becomes the cosine similarity of their **BGE embeddings** (bge-base-en-v1.5). PKS is averaged within each chunk. In this variant, internal attention only chooses *which* pair to compare. The comparison itself is an external semantic-similarity model.
- **AARF** (§4.3): during decoding, if a token's $H_t$ exceeds τ, the outputs of the selected heads are multiplied by a constant > 1 and the selected FFNs by a constant in (0,1). The text calls these α₂/β₂ and Appendix I calls them α₁/β₁. Settings are 5/0.2 on RAGTruth and 2/0.5 on Dolly (AC), with τ between 0.0 and 0.6. No weights are updated.

### Detection and mitigation results

Table 1 (p. 10) reports AUC, PCC, Recall and F1. §5.1 also lists Accuracy as a metric, but the table has no Acc column. The parsed table does not label its three blocks by model. The order in §5.1 suggests Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B, then Llama3-8B; this is an inference from that order.

| AUC, best ReDeEP vs best baseline | RAGTruth | Dolly (AC) |
|---|---|---|
| Block 1 (Llama2-7B?) | 0.7458 vs 0.7290 (RAGAS) | 0.7949 vs 0.7110 (Trulens) |
| Block 2 (Llama2-13B?) | 0.8244 vs 0.8089 (SEP) | 0.8420 vs 0.7214 (EigenScore) |
| Block 3 (Llama3-8B?) | 0.7522 (token) vs 0.7092 (SAPLMA) | 0.7354 vs 0.7040 (Trulens) |

- **Size of the margins.** The margins are much larger on Dolly (AC) than on RAGTruth, and Dolly (AC) is the dataset tuned by twofold validation with labels the authors produced themselves. The paper reports no variance, seeds or significance tests, so "significantly outperforms" is not a statistical claim.
- **Recall and F1.** ReDeEP is not best everywhere. On RAGTruth block 2, LMvLM has higher recall (0.8357 vs 0.7440). On block 3 Dolly (AC), RAGAS has 0.8000 recall against 0.8392.
- **Chunk versus token.** "ReDeEP(chunk) generally outperforms ReDeEP(token)" (p. 9) does not hold for RAGTruth block 3, where token wins on all four metrics.
- **Identical baselines.** Perplexity, LN-Entropy, Energy and SelfCheckGPT have identical numbers in blocks 1 and 2, but Focus differs between them. The paper does not explain this. Either these baselines were not rerun for the second backbone, or the blocks were copied.
- **Ablation (Appendix J, Table 3).** Only-ECS comes close to Full: token-level RAGTruth AUC is 0.7234 vs 0.7325 and 0.8040 vs 0.8181. Only-ECS already beats every baseline in RAGTruth block 3. On Dolly (AC) chunk block 3, Only-PKS reaches 0.7334 vs Full 0.7354. Adding the second covariate always helps, but by roughly 0.01–0.04 AUC in most cells, with no error bars.
- **Efficiency (Appendix K, Fig. 7).** The authors state that chunk is faster than token, and that methods without external models (ITI, ReDeEP) are faster than LLM-judge methods. The figure's values cannot be read from the parsed text.
- **AARF (Fig. 6).** GPT-4o judged pairs (AARF vs baseline) using the prompt in Appendix L, with "Tie … generally not needed". The win/tie/loss counts appear only in the figure, and the text says only "to a certain extent". There is no human evaluation and no hallucination rate.

### Related Work

The paper sits where three lines of work meet. The first is hallucination detection, in the three causal families it defines: hidden-state probes such as SAPLMA, SEP, ITI and EigenScore; context-versus-response judges such as RAGAS, Trulens, RefChecker, ChainPoll and LMvLM; and uncertainty and sampling methods such as Perplexity, LN-Entropy, Energy, Focus and SelfCheckGPT. The second is knowledge-conflict research (Xu et al. 2024), which it uses to motivate separating RAG hallucination from conflict. The third is circuit-style mechanistic interpretability: Copying Heads via OV circuits (Elhage et al.), FFNs as key-value memories (Geva et al.), the logit lens, and early-exit decoding (DoLa). Retrieval heads (Wu et al. 2024) and the study by Wadhwa et al. 2024 on how RAG balances context and parametric knowledge are its nearest mechanistic neighbours. Neither is used as a baseline.

### The boundary of the conclusion

- **Where the mechanism comes from.** The mechanistic claim, that Copying Heads lose external information and Knowledge FFNs over-inject, rests entirely on Llama2-7B (§3, Appendix C–E). Llama2-13B and Llama3-8B only inherit it through the detector working. Since the head and layer sets chosen per setting range from 1 to 30 components (Appendix I), detector performance cannot confirm that the same components play the same role in other models.
- **What "causally related" rests on.** The Finding box on p. 7 says "causally related", but its support is RQ2: destructive noise and a 10× amplification, with NLL on truthful text as the outcome (Appendix D). That establishes that the components matter for faithful copying. It does not establish that hallucinations happen *because* their contribution varies naturally. The "lost rather than mis-attended" half of the Finding rests on a single GPT-4o-judged proportion (77.5%, Table 2).
- **Whether decoupling explains the gains.** The paper attributes ReDeEP's gains to decoupling the two scores as covariates (§5.2). Its own ablation (Table 3) shows ECS alone carries most of the performance. The chunk variant's ECS is BGE embedding similarity, which is close in kind to the ECP baselines the paper argues are confounded. So the evidence supports "an attention-guided context-similarity score is a strong detector", and supports the confounding-based argument only weakly.
- **Labels and data.** Labels for Llama3-8B on RAGTruth, and for Dolly (AC) responses, come from three graduate annotators hired by the authors (Appendix G). Inter-annotator agreement is not reported, and dataset sizes are not given in the text. The largest margins (Dolly (AC)) sit on these labels and on twofold-validated hyperparameters.
- **Unused evidence.** RQ3 (Fig. 5 right) is said to "support leveraging our Finding to detect RAG hallucination". However, no part of the detector uses whether the model already knows the answer, so the claim has nothing under it in §4–5. In the other direction, the 22.5% mis-attended cases in Table 2 are never used. AARF only amplifies heads, which would not help when the heads attend to the wrong span.
- **Scope of AARF.** Calling AARF a hallucination reducer rests only on GPT-4o pairwise preferences with unreported counts. It may be cited as a proof of concept, not as a measured reduction in hallucination rate.

# LettuceDetect: A Hallucination Detection Framework for RAG Applications

## Summary

- **Background**: Even with retrieved context, RAG answers still hallucinate. Existing detectors are either LLM judges, which are slow and large, or encoders with short context windows.
- **Gap**: No permissively licensed, compact encoder detector that reads a whole RAGTruth context in one pass.
- **Research Question**: Can a ModernBERT token classifier, without NLI pretraining, match fine-tuned LLM detectors on RAGTruth?
- **Methods**: ModernBERT-base (150M) and -large (396M) are fine-tuned as token classifiers on RAGTruth and evaluated on its test split. Baseline scores are copied from the Luna, RAGTruth and RAG-HAT papers.
- **Key Findings**:
    - lettucedetect-large-v1 reaches 79.22 example-level F1, ahead of Luna (65.4) and fine-tuned Llama-2-13B (78.7), but behind RAG-HAT (83.9).
    - At span level it reaches 58.93 F1, against 52.7 for Llama-2-13B.
- **Limitations**:
    - The span-level win compares the authors' own metric implementation against numbers produced by RAGTruth's code.
    - The speed and size advantages are asserted, not measured against any baseline.
    - Nothing isolates long context as the reason for the gain, and nothing tests the model outside RAGTruth.

## Details

### What the design bets on

The paper sets out two limits of earlier detectors: encoders have short context windows and LLM judges are expensive (abstract, p. 1). Its answer is ModernBERT, which supports 8,192 tokens through RoPE and alternating local-global attention (§2, p. 2). Training uses only the binary hallucinated/supported label. RAGTruth's four hallucination types are ignored (§3, p. 4). The input is context, question and answer joined with [CLS]/[SEP] and truncated at 4,096 tokens, so the full 8k is not used (§4, p. 4). Context and question tokens are masked with label −100, and answer tokens are labelled 0/1. Training uses AdamW at lr 1e-5 with weight decay 0.01, for 6 epochs at batch size 8 on one A100. Consecutive tokens above 0.5 probability are merged into spans. Unlike Luna and RAGHalu, the model gets no NLI pretraining.

The authors measured the token lengths of RAGTruth themselves: mean 801, median 741, max 2,632 (p. 4). So every example fits easily within the 4,096-token limit. Any 4k-context encoder would see whole inputs here, and the 8k capacity does nothing on this benchmark.

### What the tables show

Data: RAGTruth (Niu et al.) has about 18k span-annotated responses across QA (MS MARCO), data-to-text (Yelp) and summarization (CNN/DM). The responses come from GPT-4, Mistral-7B and Llama-2 chat models. Train and test share these generators and tasks.

Example level (Table 2, p. 5): large-v1 reaches P 80.44, R 78.05, F1 79.22, and base-v1 reaches F1 76.07. Large-v1 beats fine-tuned Llama-2-13B on every task, but only narrowly: 70.18 vs 68.2 on QA, 88.54 vs 88.1 on data-to-text and 59.69 vs 59.1 on summarization. RAG-HAT, a DPO-trained Llama-3-8B, beats it on all three tasks. Against the best prompt baseline, gpt-4-turbo at 63.4, the gap is large. The paper does not say how an example-level label is derived from token predictions.

Span level (Table 3, p. 5): large-v1 reaches 58.93 F1 against 52.7 for Llama-2-13B, using character-level overlap. Summarization is the weak spot, with recall of 35.47 for large-v1 and 28.08 for base-v1. On summarization, base-v1 (36.71) falls below Llama-2-13B (38.6).

### Related Work

The paper places itself among three lines of work: prompt-based judges (RAGAS, Trulens, SelfCheckGPT, ChainPoll, LM-vs-LM), fine-tuned LLM judges (RAGTruth's Llama-2-13B, RAG-HAT) and encoder detectors (RAGHalu, Luna, FACTOID). It names Luna as its closest neighbour. Luna is a DeBERTa model with NLI pretraining, trained on GPT-4-annotated cross-domain QA data. LettuceDetect differs by using a ModernBERT backbone, skipping NLI pretraining, and training only on RAGTruth's human labels.

### The boundary of the conclusion

- **Baselines.** Every baseline number in Tables 2 and 3 is copied from the Luna, RAGTruth or RAG-HAT papers, and none was re-run (§5, p. 5). The 0.5-point lead over Llama-2-13B is a single run with no variance reported. That margin cannot carry "outperforms".
- **Span-level metric.** The span-level "state of the art" relies on the authors' own implementation of the metric, because RAGTruth did not release one (p. 6). The comparison therefore puts their metric next to RAGTruth's published numbers, which were produced by a possibly different procedure.
- **Efficiency.** The claim of 30 to 60 examples per second (p. 5) comes with no GPU model, batch size or input length. No baseline's throughput was measured either. The comparison against LLM judges is therefore argued, not shown.
- **"30× smaller".** The ratio holds against the 13B model, at roughly 33×. Against RAG-HAT's 8B, the only model that beats LettuceDetect, it is about 20×.
- **Abstract figures.** The "14.8% improvement" over Luna does not match Table 2: the gap is 13.8 points, or about 21% relative. The abstract also says "most prompt-based models", while §5 says "all".
- **Long context.** The paper's main motivation is long context, but nothing tests it. There is no ablation with truncated context and no comparison against a backbone with a shorter window. As noted above, RAGTruth inputs never exceed 2,632 tokens, so the benchmark cannot test the 8k capacity anyway. The gain could equally come from ModernBERT pretraining or from training on human labels.
- **Checkpoint selection.** The best checkpoint was chosen by token-level F1 (p. 4), but the paper does not say which split was used. If no held-out split was used, the reported test scores may be optimistic.
- **Scope.** The evidence covers English, in-distribution RAGTruth only. Performance on new generators, other domains or other benchmarks is untested.

# SelfCheckGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models

## Summary

- **Background**: Detecting LLM hallucinations has relied on token probabilities, which APIs may not expose, or on fact verification against an external database.
- **Gap**: The paper sets out to detect hallucinations when only the generated text is available and no external knowledge source is used.
- **Research Question**: Can consistency between one LLM response and N stochastically re-sampled responses to the same prompt flag non-factual sentences and rank passages by factuality?
- **Methods**: GPT-3 (text-davinci-003) wrote 238 WikiBio-style biographies, and the authors hand-labelled their 1,908 sentences. Five consistency scorers (BERTScore, QA, n-gram, NLI, Prompt) were compared against GPT-3's own token probabilities and against LLaMA/OPT proxy LLMs.
- **Key Findings**:
    - SelfCheckGPT-Prompt reached 93.42 AUC-PR for non-factual sentences, against 83.21 for GPT-3's Avg(−log p), with a random baseline of 72.96.
    - At passage level, Prompt correlated with human scores at Pearson 78.32, and NLI came close at 74.14 for much less compute.
    - Proxy-LLM probabilities were near random or even negatively correlated.
- **Limitations**:
    - The evidence comes from one generator (text-davinci-003) on one genre (biographies), so the claim that it works for "any black-box LLM" is untested.
    - The headline Prompt scores use ChatGPT as the judge, so they do not show a model checking itself.
    - On the harder subset that excludes fully fabricated passages, every method falls to 53 AUC-PR or below.
    - Giving the same scorers the real Wikipedia paragraph beats self-sampling for NLI and Prompt.

## Details

### How hallucination was operationalised

The prompt was "This is a Wikipedia passage about {concept}:". The 238 concepts were sampled at random from the 20% longest WikiBio test articles, to avoid obscure subjects (§6, p. 5). The main response was generated at temperature 0, and the N=20 comparison samples at temperature 1.0 (§7, p. 6).

Each sentence was labelled Major Inaccurate (1, unrelated to the topic), Minor Inaccurate (0.5) or Accurate (0). Annotators checked facts with Wikipedia or Google (Figure 3). The split was 39.9% major, 33.1% minor and 27.0% accurate, so non-factual sentences are the majority class. That is why the random AUC-PR for NonFact is already 72.96.

Only 201 of the 1,908 sentences were double-annotated. On those, Cohen's κ was 0.595 for 3 classes and 0.748 for 2 classes, and disagreements were resolved to the worse label. The paper does not say how many annotators there were or who they were. The other ~89% of the labels rest on a single judgement.

Passage scores are the average of the sentence labels. Their histogram has a large peak at 1.0, which the authors call "total hallucination" (Figure 4, p. 6). The NonFact* task removes these passages (leaving 206 passages and 1,632 sentences) and asks for major-inaccurate sentences only.

### The scorers and what they are compared against

Every variant outputs a per-sentence score $S(i)\in[0,1]$ (§5, pp. 3–5):

- **BERTScore** (RoBERTa-Large): one minus the mean of each sample's best-matching sentence score.
- **QA**: MQAG questions are generated from the sentence and answered against each sample. Inconsistency is scored with a Bayesian formula plus answerability soft-counting, with $\beta_1=\beta_2=0.8$ (App. B).
- **n-gram**: an n-gram LM is trained on the samples plus R, and scores the sentence by the average or maximum of $-\log \tilde p$.
- **NLI**: DeBERTa-v3-large fine-tuned on MNLI gives P(contradict), normalised over the entailment and contradiction logits only.
- **Prompt**: the model is asked "Is the sentence supported by the context above? Answer Yes or No", with Yes=0, No=1 and N/A=0.5.

The grey-box baselines use GPT-3's own log-probabilities. Entropy is computed from only the top-5 tokens the API returns, so the entropy baselines are truncated (Table 2 note). The black-box baselines are proxy LLMs: LLaMA 7–30B, OPT, GPT-J and NeoX.

Kadavath et al.'s self-evaluation and Kuhn et al.'s semantic uncertainty are discussed in §2 but were not run. The only black-box competitor actually tested is the proxy LLM, and it fails badly.

### What came back

Results are in Table 2 (p. 7):

| Method | NonFact | NonFact* | Factual | Pearson |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| GPT-3 Avg(−log p) | 83.21 | 38.89 | 53.97 | 57.04 |
| GPT-3 Max(−log p) | 87.51 | 35.88 | 50.46 | 57.83 |
| SelfCk-BERTScore | 81.96 | 45.96 | 44.23 | 58.18 |
| SelfCk-QA | 84.26 | 40.06 | 48.14 | 61.07 |
| SelfCk-Unigram (max) | 85.63 | 41.04 | 58.47 | 64.71 |
| SelfCk-NLI | 92.50 | 45.17 | 66.08 | 74.14 |
| SelfCk-Prompt | 93.42 | 53.19 | 67.09 | 78.32 |

- **BERTScore, QA and the strong baseline.** The authors write that BERTScore, QA and n-gram "outperform the grey-box approaches in most setups". The table supports that only weakly. On NonFact and Factual, BERTScore and QA lose to GPT-3's Max or Avg(−log p), and BERTScore's passage-level margin is 0.35 points. The clear wins are NLI and Prompt.
- **n-gram.** Max beats Avg, and performance falls as n rises from 1 to 5 (Table 7).
- **Proxy LLMs.** Avg(−log p) correlates negatively with human judgement for every OPT, GPT-J and NeoX model, and for LLaMA-7B (Table 8).
- **Number of samples.** Performance rises smoothly with diminishing returns, and n-gram needs the most samples (Figure 7). The values are only plotted, not tabulated.
- **Who checks.** Table 2's Prompt row uses ChatGPT (gpt-3.5-turbo) as the checker. With N=4, GPT-3 judging its own text gets Pearson 73.11, against 76.47 for ChatGPT (Table 4).
- **Agreement between judges.** GPT-3 and ChatGPT agreed on about 82% of 7,632 Yes/No calls (Table 6). The table's row/column orientation is not labelled.
- **Cost.** Prompt with N=20 over all sentences was estimated at about $200 with GPT-3 and about $20 with ChatGPT (App. C).

### Self-samples versus external knowledge

When the actual WikiBio first paragraph replaces the samples (Table 3, p. 8), results split by scorer:

- **Prompt** gains on every metric: NonFact* rises from 53.19 to 65.26 and Pearson from 78.32 to 85.90.
- **NLI** gains on every metric except NonFact, where it slips slightly from 92.50 to 91.18.
- **BERTScore and QA** are roughly unchanged.
- **Unigram** collapses, because one paragraph is too little text to train an n-gram model.

So for the two strongest scorers, self-consistency stands in for retrieval rather than matching it.

### Related Work

The paper positions itself along four lines:

- hallucination in NLG (summarisation, dialogue);
- sequence-level uncertainty estimation (token probability or entropy, semantic uncertainty);
- multi-stage fact verification against retrieved evidence;
- LLM self-evaluation and probes on internal states.

It sets itself against two of these explicitly. Azaria & Mitchell's classifier on hidden states needs white-box access and labelled data. Liu et al.'s detection benchmark uses perturbed text rather than real LLM output.

### Discussion

The authors read the n-gram (max) result to mean that a token appearing once or rarely across 20 samples is a strong hallucination signal (p. 7). They attribute the proxy LLMs' failure to differences in generation style between models, which they offer as an explanation without testing it.

They recommend NLI as the practical trade-off between performance and compute. No runtime is measured for NLI, so that recommendation rests on its architecture rather than on numbers.

### The boundary of the conclusion

- **Scope.** The claim is general detection for black-box LLMs. The evidence is one 2023 generator writing one genre, with concepts chosen to be well covered by pre-training.
- **Where the margins come from.** Total hallucinations, where the samples obviously disagree, seem to drive much of the gap. On NonFact*, the best method reaches 53.19 against a random 29.72, while the headline passage-level correlations are computed over a bimodal distribution (Figure 4).
- **No held-out data.** The paper never mentions a dev split. Unigram-max (Table 7), soft-counting (Table 5) and the β values appear to have been chosen on the same 238 passages they are reported on.
- **"Self" check.** The headline Prompt number uses a different, stronger model as the judge (Table 4). The pure self-check rests on a single N=4 comparison.
- **Consistent errors.** The method's premise is that consistency signals factuality. No experiment isolates facts that are wrong but sampled consistently, which this method cannot catch by construction.
- **Label reliability.** The κ of 0.595 on the 3-class scheme concerns exactly the minor/major boundary that NonFact* depends on.
- **Unused evidence.** Table 3 shows that retrieval, when available, beats self-sampling for the best scorers. The conclusion carries this forward only as "external databases are infeasible for every use case", a claim the paper argues rather than tests.

## REDEEP: DETECTING HALLUCINATION IN RETRIEVAL-AUGMENTED GENERATION VIA MECHANISTIC INTERPRETABILITY

Zhongxiang Sun1∗, Xiaoxue Zang2, Kai Zheng2, Jun Xu1† Xiao Zhang1, Weijie Yu 3, Yang Song 2, Han Li 2

1Gaoling School of Artificial Intelligence, Renmin University of China, Beijing, China 2Kuaishou Technology Co., Ltd., Beijing, China 3School of Information Technology and Management, University of International Business and Economics sunzhongxiang@ruc.edu.cn

ABSTRACT

Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models are designed to incorporate external knowledge, reducing hallucinations caused by insufficient parametric (internal) knowledge. However, even with accurate and relevant retrieved content, RAG models can still produce hallucinations by generating outputs that conflict with the retrieved information. Detecting such hallucinations requires disentangling how Large Language Models (LLMs) utilize external and parametric knowledge. Current detection methods often focus on one of these mechanisms or without decoupling their intertwined effects, making accurate detection difficult. In this paper, we investigate the internal mechanisms behind hallucinations in RAG scenarios. We discover hallucinations occur when the Knowledge FFNs in LLMs overemphasize parametric knowledge in the residual stream, while Copying Heads fail to effectively retain or integrate external knowledge from retrieved content. Based on these findings, we propose ReDeEP, a novel method that detects hallucinations by decoupling LLM’s utilization of external context and parametric knowledge. Our experiments show that ReDeEP significantly improves RAG hallucination detection accuracy. Additionally, we introduce AARF, which mitigates hallucinations by modulating the contributions of Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads.

(i): parametric knowledge is confounded by external context, (ii): external context is confounded by parametric knowledge, and (iii): mixes both without decoupling their contributions. (Ours): decouple these confounders using mechanistic interpretability, incorporating them as covariates to improve hallucination detection. LLMs have made significant advancements in natural language processing tasks (Dubey et al., 2024; Achiam et al., 2023). However, they still face challenges with hallucinations, often generating factually inaccurate outputs (Huang et al., 2023). To mitigate this issue, many researchers have introduced Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) models, which aim to improve the accuracy of LLM responses by incorporating relevant information retrieved from external knowledge bases (Shuster et al., 2021; Gao et al., 2023). Despite the use of accurate and relevant retrieved context, RAG models may still produce statements that are either unsupported or contradict the retrieved information, a phenomenon we term RAG Hallucination (Niu et al., 2024; Magesh et al., 2024). Recent studies have examined the potential conflicts between the external context and the LLM’s parametric knowledge in RAG models (Xu et al., 2024). As shown in Figure 1, these conflicts can lead to hallucinations but do not always cause them. Therefore, it is important to distinguish RAG hallucination from Knowledge Conflict as a new research direction. Our work focuses on detecting RAG hallucinations, specifically in cases where the retrieved external context is accurate and relevant. Existing hallucination detection methods can be categorized into three causal frameworks (Neuberg, 2003; Pearl, 2009), as illustrated in Figure 2 (detailed introduction of methods see Appendix H): (i) Parametric Confounded by External: which relies on the LLM’s hidden states for hallucination detection, where the external context (E) serves as a confounder between parametric knowledge (P) and hallucinations (H). From a knowledge storage perspective (Geva et al., 2021), hidden states represent the result of querying the parametric knowledge (P) with external context (E), establishing a causal path from E to P (graph (a)). The presence of E as a confounder complicates the accurate prediction of hallucinations based on P alone (Chyzhyk et al., 2022). (ii) External Confounded by Parametric: which focuses on hallucination detection by leveraging external context and model responses. Here, parametric knowledge (P) is a confounder between the external context (E) and hallucinations (H), creating a causal link from P to E (graph (b)) due to the unavoidable presence of parametric knowledge in the response. (iii) Mixed Parametric and External: which combines both parametric and external knowledge directly, often using uncertainty or sampling techniques (e.g., token probability) to detect hallucinations (graph (c)). However, this mixing of E and P without decoupling their roles obscures their individual contributions (Bengio et al., 2013). To address the challenges of hallucination detection in RAG models, we first leverage mechanistic interpretability (Ferrando et al., 2024; Elhage et al., 2021) to decouple the LLM’s utilization of parametric knowledge and external context. Specifically, we conduct an empirical study to explore the internal mechanisms behind hallucination generation in RAG scenarios. We introduce two metrics: the External Context Score, which uses attention heads to quantify the model’s utilization on external context, and the Parametric Knowledge Score, which is based on FFNs to evaluate LLM’s utilization of parametric knowledge (§ 3.1). Correlation analysis and causal intervention reveals that hallucinations typically occur when Knowledge FFNs (from later LLM layers) over-add parametric knowledge into the residual stream, while Copying Heads (attention heads exhibiting

copying behaviours) neglect the necessary external knowledge from retrieved content or LLM loses the information attended to by Copying Heads during the generation process (§ 3.2). Building on our causal analysis and mechanistic interpretability, we propose ReDeEP (Regressing Decoupled External context score and Parametric knowledge score) for detecting hallucinations in LLM-based RAG, which treat parametric knowledge (P) and external context (E) as covariates to solve the confounding problem (Kahlert et al., 2017) (see Ours in Figure 2). Additionally, we introduce AARF (Add Attention Reduce FFN), which mitigates hallucinations by modulating the contributions of Knowledge FFNs and Copying Heads in the residual stream (§ 4). Experiments on RAGTruth and Dolly (AC) confirm that ReDeEP significantly outperforms existing detection methods, while AARF improves the truthfulness of LLaMA models (§ 5).

2 BACKGROUND AND RELATED WORKS

2.1 BACKGROUND

Our work is grounded in mechanistic interpretability (Ferrando et al., 2024; nostalgebraist, 2020; Meng et al., 2022; Elhage et al., 2021), which aims to explain how individual components of language models (LMs) contribute to predictions. In this study, we focus on transformer decoder-only architectures (GPT-like models) due to their widespread use (Achiam et al., 2023; Dubey et al., 2024). Transformers use residual connections, where each layer adds information from Attention Heads and Feed-Forward Networks (FFNs) to the hidden state via the residual stream, contributing to the final prediction (Elhage et al., 2021). Attention Heads: Attention heads play a crucial role in contextualizing token representations by selectively attending to previous tokens and updating the residual stream (Ferrando & Voita, 2024; Clark et al., 2019; Wu et al., 2024). Notably, some attention heads, referred to as Copying Heads, have been shown to copy information from one token to another through their OV (output-value) circuits (Elhage et al., 2021). These heads can be identified by analyzing the positive eigenvalues of the OV matrix, which indicate copying behavior. Copying Heads contributes to preserving previously attended tokens in the residual stream, which is critical for external context utilization. FFNs: FFN layers primarily function as knowledge storage in transformers (Geva et al., 2021). Each FFN layer transforms the hidden state by linearly combining key-value pairs, where keys encode specific knowledge and values represent the output of this knowledge. Research shows that FFNs are critical for the utilization of parametric knowledge within LLMs, enabling the model to retrieve and integrate stored information effectively for prediction (Dai et al., 2022). Logit Lens: The LogitLens is a technique that decodes hidden states xl directly into the vocabulary distribution using the LayerNorm and the unembedding matrix WU of the LLM for interpretability (nostalgebraist, 2020): LogitLens xl = LayerNorm(xl)WU . (1)

By understanding the roles of Attention Heads (e.g., Copying Heads) and FFNs, we can better interpret the internal states of LLMs and identify the mechanisms behind hallucinations in RAG scenarios. Detailed background information can be found in Appendix A.

2.2 RELATED WORK

Hallucination of LLMs: LLMs often generate hallucinations—content inconsistent with real-world facts or inputs (Huang et al., 2023). As depicted in Figure 2, although there has been extensive research on detecting hallucinations (Niu et al., 2024; Manakul et al., 2023; Han et al., 2024), few studies have concentrated on RAG hallucinations, particularly on the internal mechanisms driving these hallucinations. Inspired by research on Knowledge Conflicts (Xu et al., 2024), our work is the first to apply mechanistic interpretability to lens the internal mechanisms of RAG hallucinations from the perspectives of LLM’s utilization of external and parametric knowledge, leading to a more accurate detection method than previous approaches. 5.1 SETTINGS

Data: We evaluate ReDePE and AARF on two public RAG hallucination datasets. RAGTruth is the first high-quality, manually annotated RAG hallucination dataset. The data includes three RAG task types: Question Answering (QA), Data-to-Text Writing, and News Summarization. Dolly (AC) is a dataset with Accurate Context obtained from (Hu et al., 2024), including tasks such as text summarization, closed-QA, and information extraction. More details of the data are in Appendix G. Baselines: We conduct experiments on three variants of LLaMA, including LLaMA2-7B-Chat, LLaMA2-13B-Chat, and LLaMA3-8B-Chat. For hallucination detection methods, we follow the classification of existing methods as shown in Figure 2. We use (1) Parametric Confounded by External Methods (PCE), (2) External Confounded by Parametric Methods (ECP), and (3) Mixed Parametric and External Methods (MPE). For detailed baselines information, see Appendix H. We used AUC, Pearson Correlation Coefficient (PCC), Accuracy (Acc.), Recall (Rec.), and F1 as evaluation metrics for detection accuracy. Implementation details are provided in Appendix I.

5.2 EXPERIMENTS

RAG Hallucination Detection: As shown in Table 1, ReDeEP consistently improves performance across two datasets, various backbone methods, and different metrics, validating its effectiveness in detecting RAG hallucinations. ReDeEP outperforms MPE methods, demonstrating that mechanistic interpretability effectively decouples the LLM’s utilization of external context and parametric knowledge, enabling more accurate detection of RAG hallucinations. Additionally, ReDeEP surpasses both ECP and PCE methods by incorporating both the External Context Score and Parametric Knowledge Score as covariates in a multivariate regression approach, effectively addressing the confounding problem. ReDeEP(chunk) generally outperforms ReDeEP(token) in most metrics, suggesting that chunk-level processing better preserves semantic integrity and improves detection performance. Further support for ReDeEP’s effectiveness is provided by the ablation study in Appendix J, while the efficiency analysis in Appendix K confirms that ReDeEP achieves comparable time efficiency to the most efficient baselines. Truthful RAG Generation: We evaluated our hallucination reduction method AARF on both the RAGTruth and Dolly (AC) datasets, using GPT-4-o for automatic evaluation to assess the truthfulness (Prompt details can be found in Appendix L). Pairwise comparisons rated by GPT-4-o are shown in Figure 6, demonstrating that AARF can reduce hallucinations to a certain extent compared to the baseline model. These results validate the effectiveness of our intervention experiments and confirm the findings presented in RQ2 of Section 3.2.

long-context awareness is an inevitable feature. Hallucination Detection can vary in granularity, ranging from example-based detection (which assesses if an answer contains hallucinations) to token, span, or sentence-level detection (Niu et al., 2024). The methods for detecting hallucinations also differ based on the techniques employed. Prompt-based Techniques typically utilize zero or few-shot large language models (LLMs) to identify hallucinations in LLM-generated responses. Few-shot or fine-tuned evaluation frameworks, such as RAGAS (Es et al., 2024), Trulens6, and ARES (Saad-Falcon et al., 2024), have emerged to provide hallucination detection at scale using LLM judges. However, real-time prediction remains a challenge for these methods. Other prompt-based approaches, like the zero-shot method SelfCheckGPT (Manakul et al., 2023), employ stochastic sampling to identify inconsistencies across multiple response variants. Rather than relying on a single prompt, Chainpoll (Friel and Sanyal, 2023) implements a series of verification steps to detect hallucinations. Cohen et al. (2023) presents a method of cross-examination between two LLMs to uncover inconsistencies. Chang et al. (2024) utilized LLM-based classifiers trained on synthetic errors to detect both hallucinations and coverage errors in LLM-generated responses. Fine-tuned LLM Judges approaches involve training LLMs on hallucination detection tasks using specific training data. Niu et al. (2024) not only introduced the RagTruth data but also presented a fine-tuned Llama-2-13B LLM, which achieved state-of-the-art performance on their test set, even surpassing larger models like GPT-4. RAG-HAT (Song et al., 2024) introduced a novel approach called Hallucination Aware Tuning (HAT), which involves training models to generate detection labels and provide detailed descriptions of identified hallucinations. They created a preference dataset to facilitate Direct Preference Optimization (DPO) training. Fine-tuning through DPO results in SOTA performance on the RAGTruth test set. Encoder-based Solutions focus on addressing computational efficiency constraints through domain-specific adaptations. RAGHalu (Zimmerman et al., 2024) employs a two-tiered encoder model that utilizes binary classification at each

6https://www.trulens.org/

layer, fine-tuning a Natural Language Inference (NLI) model based on DeBERTa (He et al., 2021). The approach most similar to our work is Luna (Belyi et al., 2025), which also builds on DeBERTa and NLI to create a lightweight longcontext hallucination detection system capable of managing longer contexts effectively. Luna draws connections between detecting entailment in NLI tasks and identifying hallucinations. They finetuned on a large, cross-domain corpus of questionanswering-based RAG samples, with annotations provided by GPT-4. During the inference phase, Luna conducts sentence- or token-level checks on each model’s response against the retrieved passages, effectively flagging unsupported fragments. FACTOID (Rawte et al., 2024) introduces a Factual Entailment (FE) framework, which represents a new form of textual entailment aimed at locating hallucinations at the token or span level. Other approaches, such as ReDeEp (Sun et al., 2025), introduce techniques to analyze internal model states for hallucination detection.

## 3 Data

We trained and evaluated our models using the RAGTruth dataset (Niu et al., 2024). RAGTruth is the first large-scale benchmark for evaluating hallucinations in RAG settings. The dataset contains 18,000 annotated examples at the span level across three tasks: question answering, data-to-text generation, and news summarization. For the question answering task, data was sampled from the MS MARCO dataset (Bajaj et al., 2018), where each question had up to three corresponding contexts. The authors then prompted LLMs to generate answers based on the retrieved passages. In the data-to-text generation task, LLMs were asked to generate reviews for sampled businesses from the Yelp Open Dataset (Yelp, 2021). For the news summarization task, randomly selected documents were taken from the training set of the CNN/Daily Mail dataset (See et al., 2017), and LLMs were prompted to create summaries. For response generation, various LLMs were employed, including GPT-4-0613 (OpenAI et al., 2024), Mistral-7B-Instruct (Jiang et al., 2023), and selections from the Llama models, such as Llama2-7b-chat and Llama-2-13B-chat (Grattafiori et al., 2024). Each sample in the dataset includes one response from each model, resulting in six responses per sample in RAGTruth.

The entire dataset was annotated by human evaluators, who marked annotations in the responses and provided rationales. RAGTruth categorizes hallucinations into types such as Evident Conflict, Subtle Conflict, Evident Introduction of Baseless Information, and Subtle Introduction of Baseless Information. For our training, we focused solely on the binary task of recognizing hallucinations without considering these specific categories. An example from the dataset can be seen in Table 1. We tokenized RAGTruth and found that the mean token length is 801 tokens, with a median of 741 tokens, a minimum of 194, and a maximum of 2632 tokens. This highlights the need for long-context models, such as ModernBERT, to effectively detect hallucinations.

## 4 Method

We trained ModernBERT-base and -large variants as token classifiers on the RAGTruth dataset. Input sequences were constructed by concatenating context, question, and answer segments using special tokens ([CLS] for context, [SEP] for separation) and tokenized to a maximum length of 4,096 tokens (in the current version we haven’t utilized ModernBERT’s full 8,192 context length). For handling tokenization, we’ve used the AutoTokenizer (Wolf et al., 2020). Our models are based solely on the ModernBERT architecture and were not pretrained on the NLI task, unlike previous encoder-based architectures.

The architecture leveraged Hugging Face’s AutoModelForTokenClassification (Wolf et al., 2020) with ModernBERT as the backbone, and a classification head on top. Context/question tokens were masked (label=-100), while answer tokens were labeled as

## SELFCHECKGPT: Zero-Resource Black-Box Hallucination Detection for Generative Large Language Models

Potsawee Manakul, Adian Liusie, Mark J. F. Gales

ALTA Institute, Department of Engineering, University of Cambridge pm574@cam.ac.uk, al826@cam.ac.uk, mjfg@eng.cam.ac.uk

Abstract

Generative Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 are capable of generating highly fluent responses to a wide variety of user prompts. However, LLMs are known to hallucinate facts and make non-factual statements which can undermine trust in their output. Existing fact-checking approaches either require access to the output probability distribution (which may not be available for systems such as ChatGPT) or external databases that are interfaced via separate, often complex, modules. In this work, we propose "SelfCheckGPT", a simple sampling-based approach that can be used to fact-check the responses of black-box models in a zero-resource fashion, i.e. without an external database. SelfCheckGPT leverages the simple idea that if an LLM has knowledge of a given concept, sampled responses are likely to be similar and contain consistent facts. However, for hallucinated facts, stochastically sampled responses are likely to diverge and contradict one another. We investigate this approach by using GPT-3 to generate passages about individuals from the WikiBio dataset, and manually annotate the factuality of the generated passages. We demonstrate that SelfCheckGPT can: i) detect non-factual and factual sentences; and ii) rank passages in terms of factuality. We compare our approach to several baselines and show that our approach has considerably higher AUC-PR scores in sentence-level hallucination detection and higher correlation scores in passage-level factuality assessment compared to grey-box methods.1

1 Introduction

Large Language Models (LLMs) such as GPT-3 (Brown et al., 2020) and PaLM (Chowdhery et al., 2022) are capable of generating fluent and realistic responses to a variety of user prompts. They have been used in many applications such as automatic

tools to draft reports, virtual assistants and summarization systems. Despite the convincing and realistic nature of LLM-generated texts, a growing concern with LLMs is their tendency to hallucinate facts. It has been widely observed that models can confidently generate fictitious information, and worryingly there are few, if any, existing approaches to suitably identify LLM hallucinations. A possible approach of hallucination detection is to leverage existing intrinsic uncertainty metrics to determine the parts of the output sequence that the system is least certain of (Yuan et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2023). However, uncertainty metrics such as token probability or entropy require access to token-level probability distributions, information which may not be available to users for example when systems are accessed through limited external APIs. An alternate approach is to leverage fact-verification approaches, where evidence is retrieved from an external database to assess the veracity of a claim (Thorne et al., 2018; Guo et al., 2022). However, facts can only be assessed relative to the knowledge present in the database. Addition1

<!-- page 2 -->

ally, hallucinations are observed over a wide range of tasks beyond pure fact verification (Kryscinski et al., 2020; Maynez et al., 2020).

In this paper, we propose SelfCheckGPT, a sampling-based approach that can detect whether responses generated by LLMs are hallucinated or factual. To the best of our knowledge, SelfCheckGPT is the first work to analyze model hallucination of general LLM responses, and is the first zero-resource hallucination detection solution that can be applied to black-box systems. The motivating idea of SelfCheckGPT is that when an LLM has been trained on a given concept, the sampled responses are likely to be similar and contain consistent facts. However, for hallucinated facts, stochastically sampled responses are likely to diverge and may contradict one another. By sampling multiple responses from an LLM, one can measure information consistency between the different responses and determine if statements are factual or hallucinated. Since SelfCheckGPT only leverages sampled responses, it has the added benefit that it can be used for black-box models, and it requires no external database. Five variants of SelfCheckGPT for measuring informational consistency are considered: BERTScore, question-answering, n-gram, NLI, and LLM prompting. Through analysis of annotated articles generated by GPT-3, we show that SelfCheckGPT is a highly effective hallucination detection method that can even outperform greybox methods, and serves as a strong first baseline for an increasingly important problem of LLMs.

2 Background and Related Work 2.1 Hallucination of Large Language Models

Hallucination has been studied in text generation tasks, including summarization (Huang et al., 2021) and dialogue generation (Shuster et al., 2021), as well as in a variety of other natural language generation tasks (Ji et al., 2023). Self-consistency decoding has shown to improve chain-of-thought prompting performance on complex reasoning tasks (Wang et al., 2023). Further, Liu et al. (2022) introduce a hallucination detection dataset, however, texts are obtained by perturbing factual texts and thus may not reflect true LLM hallucination. Recently, Azaria and Mitchell (2023) trained a multi-layer perception classifier where an LLM’s hidden representations are used as inputs to predict the truthfulness of a sentence. However, this approach is a white-box approach that uses the

internal states of the LLM, which may not be available through API calls, and requires labelled data for supervised training. Another recent approach is self-evaluation (Kadavath et al., 2022), where an LLM is prompted to evaluate its previous prediction, e.g., to predict the probability that its generated response/answer is true. 2.2 Sequence Level Uncertainty Estimation Token probabilities have been used as an indication of model certainty. For example, OpenAI’s GPT-3 web interface allows users to display token probabilities (as shown in Figure 2), and further uncertainty estimation approaches based on aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty have been studied for autoregressive generation (Xiao and Wang, 2021; Malinin and Gales, 2021). Additionally, conditional language model scores have been used to evaluate properties of texts (Yuan et al., 2021; Fu et al., 2023). Recently, semantic uncertainty has been proposed to address uncertainty in free-form generation tasks where probabilities are attached to concepts instead of tokens (Kuhn et al., 2023).

Figure 2: Example of OpenAI’s GPT-3 web interface with output token-level probabilities displayed.

## 2.3 Fact Verification

Existing fact-verification approaches follow a multi-stage pipeline of claim detection, evidence retrieval and verdict prediction (Guo et al., 2022; Zhong et al., 2020). Such methods, however, require access to external databases and can have considerable inference costs.

3 Grey-Box Factuality Assessment

This section will introduce methods that can be used to determine the factuality of LLM responses in a zero-resource setting when one has full access

to output distributions.2 We will use ‘factual’ to define when statements are grounded in valid information, i.e. when hallucinations are avoided, and ‘zero-resource’ when no external database is used. 3.1 Uncertainty-based Assessment To understand how the factuality of a generated response can be determined in a zero-resource setting, we consider LLM pre-training. During pretraining, the model is trained with next-word prediction over massive corpora of textual data. This gives the model a strong understanding of language (Jawahar et al., 2019; Raffel et al., 2020), powerful contextual reasoning (Zhang et al., 2020), as well as world knowledge (Liusie et al., 2023). Consider the input "Lionel Messi is a _". Since Messi is a world-famous athlete who may have appeared multiple times in pre-training, the LLM is likely to know who Messi is. Therefore given the context, the token "footballer" may be assigned a high probability while other professions such as "carpenter" may be considered improbable. However, for a different input such as "John Smith is a _", the system will be unsure of the continuation which may result in a flat probability distribution. During inference, this is likely to lead to a non-factual word being generated. This insight allows us to understand the connection between uncertainty metrics and factuality. Factual sentences are likely to contain tokens with higher likelihood and lower entropy, while hallucinations are likely to come from positions with flat probability distributions with high uncertainty. 4 Black-Box Factuality Assessment

A drawback of grey-box methods is that they require output token-level probabilities. Though this may seem a reasonable requirement, for massive LLMs only available through limited API calls, such token-level information may not be available (such as with ChatGPT). Therefore, we consider black-box approaches which remain applicable even when only text-based responses are available.

## Proxy LLMs

A simple approach to approximate the grey-box approaches is by using a proxy LLM, i.e. another LLM that we have full access to, such as LLaMA (Touvron et al., 2023). A proxy LLM can be used to approximate the output token-level probabilities of the black-box LLM generating the text. In the next section, we propose SelfCheckGPT, which is also a black-box approach.

## 5 SelfCheckGPT

SelfCheckGPT is our proposed black-box zeroresource hallucination detection scheme, which operates by comparing multiple sampled responses and measuring consistency.

SelfCheckGPT draws a further N stochastic LLM response samples {S 1, S2, ..., Sn, ..., SN } using the same query, and then measures the consistency between the response and the stochastic samples. Given samples {S1, ..., SN } generated by an LLM, one can use the samples to create a new language model that approximates the LLM. I compared the three papers tagged *detection* in your library. I read each paper's method and evaluation sections for this. Ragas and ARES also score whether an answer is faithful to its sources, but they're tagged *evaluation*, so I left them out.

| | [Manakul et al. 2023](owlit://library/arxiv-2303.08896) SelfCheckGPT | [Kovács & Recski 2025](owlit://library/arxiv-2502.17125) LettuceDetect | [Sun et al. 2024](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414) ReDeEP |
|---|---|---|---|
| **What "unsupported" means** | Not consistent with the model's own other answers. No source document is used. | Not supported by the retrieved context | Contradicts or isn't supported by a retrieved context that is correct |
| **How it decides** | Samples N more answers to the same prompt (N=20) and scores each sentence by how much the samples disagree with it. There are five ways to score: BERTScore, QA, n-gram, NLI contradiction, or asking an LLM "Is the sentence supported by the context above?" ([p.3–5](owlit://library/arxiv-2303.08896#p5)) | A ModernBERT token classifier reads the context, question and answer and labels each answer token supported (0) or hallucinated (1). Neighbouring tokens above 0.5 are merged into spans ([p.4](owlit://library/arxiv-2502.17125#p4)) | Combines two scores. ECS: does the model's output stay close to the context its copying heads attend to? PKS: how much do late FFN layers change the next-token distribution? An answer is flagged when PKS is high and ECS is low ([p.8](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414#p8)) |
| **How fine-grained** | Each sentence, averaged for the whole passage | Each token or span, plus the whole answer | Each token or chunk, averaged for the whole answer |
| **Labels needed** | None. Human labels are used only to evaluate | Yes: RAGTruth's human span labels, used for full training | A few. Labelled RAGTruth training data picks the heads and layers ([p.4–7](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414#p4)), and a labelled validation set sets the weights and how many heads and layers to use ([p.21](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414#p21)) |
| **Second model needed** | Depends on the scorer: RoBERTa (BERTScore), a DeBERTa NLI model, a QA model, or an LLM judge. With the prompt scorer the judge was GPT-3 or ChatGPT ([p.6](owlit://library/arxiv-2303.08896#p6)) | The fine-tuned classifier itself (150M or 396M parameters). The generator isn't needed | The token version needs none. The chunk version compares chunks with a BGE embedding model ([p.8](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414#p8)) |
| **Access to internals** | None. It only needs to sample text, so it works on black-box models | None. It needs only the text | Full white-box access to the model that wrote the answer: attention weights, hidden states, and the residual stream before and after each FFN |
| **Tested on** | 238 WikiBio-style biographies written by GPT-3 (text-davinci-003), with 1,908 sentences labelled by hand. There is no retrieved context ([p.5](owlit://library/arxiv-2303.08896#p5)) | RAGTruth test split only (QA, data-to-text, summarization). The answers come from GPT-4, Mistral-7B and Llama-2. All baseline scores are copied from earlier papers ([p.3–5](owlit://library/arxiv-2502.17125#p5)) | RAGTruth and Dolly (AC), each with Llama2-7B, Llama2-13B and Llama3-8B, against 16 baselines ([p.9](owlit://library/arxiv-2410.11414#p9)) |

**What this means for comparing them:**
- **Only two of them check against a source.** SelfCheckGPT tests whether the model is consistent with itself, not whether the answer is grounded in a document. When the authors gave it the real Wikipedia paragraph instead of the samples, the NLI and prompt scorers improved ([p.8](owlit://library/arxiv-2303.08896#p8)). Of the three, only LettuceDetect and ReDeEP test against retrieved context.
- **What each one needs grows from left to right:** SelfCheckGPT needs only text, LettuceDetect needs labelled training data, and ReDeEP needs labels plus white-box access to the model that wrote the answer. Only ReDeEP has to run inside that same model.
- **Only partly comparable.** LettuceDetect and ReDeEP both use RAGTruth. However, ReDeEP reports AUC for each backbone model, while LettuceDetect reports F1 over the pooled responses from all the generators. Their numbers can't be lined up directly. Two caveats, both from Owlit's digests of these papers: ReDeEP's own ablation shows that ECS alone does most of the work, and neither paper is tested outside the data it was tuned on.
